title: How Desert Mosses Use Brief Rainfall
passage:
In dry regions, some mosses survive by treating rainfall as a brief opportunity rather than a lasting supply. Their leaves absorb water rapidly, and shallow colonies spread across soil and rock, allowing many plants to benefit from a small shower. When the surface dries, the mosses enter dormancy, and growth nearly stops. This strategy keeps them alive through long intervals without the continuous water required by larger plants.

A moss colony also changes the ground around it. Its tangled stems slow moving water, while spaces among them hold moisture against evaporation. The colony can keep upper soil damp briefly after rain ends. Its stems also trap dust and organic particles that later become nutrients. These effects do not create a permanent wet habitat, but they make the surface more favorable for mosses and nearby small organisms.

Timing is especially important. During a shower, moss tissues swell and begin photosynthesis soon afterward. If sunlight returns quickly, the colony can produce energy before stored water disappears. Several brief showers may make a colony more productive than one long event containing the same total water, because repeated wetting allows photosynthesis to resume multiple times.

This pattern shows why survival and growth differ. Dormancy protects mosses during harsh conditions, while rapid activity helps them use temporary improvements. They do not overcome desert dryness; instead, they combine water-saving structures with quick responses to change. Their success depends on matching each phase of activity to limited opportunities in the environment.
